chs.experience: Start with hands-on IT practice: in Computer Engineering or Exploring Computer Science, focus on computer setup, troubleshooting basic networking issues, and learn about ethical use of digital resources. Make the most of labs and simulations—ask your teachers for extra practice with secure environments. As you continue, engage in projects or competitions about digital safety, or interview local IT staff about their real challenges (with supervision and permission).

future_course_details.name: Intro to Computing Concepts
future_course_details.planning_note: Course completion and placement are unknown. Confirm level, eligibility and schedule with your counselor.

future_course_details.why: Intro to Computing Concepts strengthens skills in programming, algorithms, software development, and data analysis, all of which are needed in cybersecurity for scripting, automation, and understanding how attacks are planned and analyzed. This is a recommended prerequisite for the main security course if not starting with Computer Engineering.

future_course_details.evidence: Networking and Cyber Security Cybersecurity gives students hands-on and career-focused skills to identify cyber threats and secure computer systems.
future_course_details.name: Networking and Cyber Security

future_course_details.planning_note: Course completion and placement are unknown. Confirm level, eligibility and schedule with your counselor.
future_course_details.why: Probability and Statistics introduces methods for analyzing data, detecting anomalies, and making quantitative decisions—skills that are increasingly important in cybersecurity roles for interpreting logs, incident trends, and threat analysis.

chs.good: Networking and Cyber Security (CHS-131) is available grades 10–12 but requires a prior computing course or teacher recommendation. You cannot take it in grade 9; instead, focus on establishing your foundation. If entering the program late, you may have less time for the complete sequence but can still access critical skills—discuss alternatives with your counselor if needed. All practice should stay within authorized labs and school settings. Source: CHS 2025–26 Program of Studies; current-year availability is not verified. Ask your counselor to confirm prerequisites, placement and pathway entry.

chs.next: In grade 9, discuss your planned computing courses and interests (especially Computer Engineering or Exploring Computer Science) with your counselor to ensure correct placement. Next year, progress to the required computing prerequisites, and build a portfolio of technical projects or problem-solving notes. Watch for safe, supervised cybersecurity scenarios in class or local events.

chs.reflection: Cybersecurity is hands-on, fast-changing, and requires both a technical toolkit and ethics. Early IT experience and a solid base in computing will help you stand out. Recognize that security is a field where responsibility and trust are as important as technical know-how.

steps: Further Education in Cybersecurity or IT

After high school, consider a 2- or 4-year degree in computer science, IT, or cybersecurity. Programs may include hands-on labs, networking, security, ethics, programming, and advanced threat analysis.

Certifications such as CompTIA Security+, Network+, or entry-level Cisco credentials (CCNA) are valued by employers and often expected in the field. They require both technical and ethical understanding.

Seek internships, part-time tech helpdesk, or junior IT roles to gain real-world experience with system security, troubleshooting, and team practice. Many entry points support progression to full cybersecurity specialist.

As new threats and technologies appear, ongoing coursework, bootcamps, or industry conferences maintain your skills and can lead to advanced roles in digital forensics, incident response, or penetration testing.
With proven technical skills, experience, and credentials, move into specialist positions protecting organizational systems, responding to threats, and staying current with evolving best practices.
summary: Cybersecurity specialists defend networks, systems, and data from threats by applying specialized skills in IT, programming, networking, and security practices. Early preparation is essential—building a strong foundation in computing concepts, computer hardware, and basic programming prepares you for advanced hands-on security tasks later in high school. Cumberland High’s catalog provides options to start exploring IT and computing skills in grade 9, followed by pathways leading to specialized security coursework by grade 10 or later.
